title: Metric ownership roster and instrumentation playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a pragmatic playbook for assigning metric/tracing ownership, standardizing instrumentation, and reducing investigation friction across inference services. It’s intended for eng-observability and service owners who ship telemetry. The goal is not to be exhaustive; it’s to minimize toil while keeping metric costs and cardinality reasonable.

Scope:
- All runtime metrics (latency, throughput, cache, batching, GPU utilization)
- Tracing anchors for end-to-end request flows and fallbacks
- Dashboard hygiene and onboarding checklist for new/changed metrics
- Lightweight cost-control guidance (label cardinality, retention suggestions)

Quick owner roster (living):
- inference.request.latency.* -> owner: Priya Nair (serving-runtime)
- inference.request.count -> owner: Ethan Rhodes (serving-runtime)
- kvcache.hit_ratio -> owner: Mariana Lopes (runtime-cache)
- batch.size.histogram -> owner: Asha Kapoor (batching)
- model.load.time -> owner: Jon Wallace (release-engineering)
- platform.gpu.utilization -> owner: Infra-SRE (rotating oncall)
Notes: Owners must appear on the metric catalog entry and accept Slack pings for their metric by default. Ownership rotates quarterly for infra oncall metrics.

Metric definition template (use for new metrics):
- name: short.snake.case (e.g., inference.request.latency.p50)
- description: one sentence purpose + how to interpret
- unit: ms | count | ratio | percent | bytes
- aggregation: gauge | counter | histogram | summary
- labels: list (note cardinality suggestions)
- owner: person/team
- alerting: suggested severity and threshold rationale
- dashboard: default dashboard/widget where it should appear
- instrumentation: repo/file + sample code / PR link

Example metric entries (illustrative):
1) inference.request.latency.p95
- description: 95th percentile end-to-end token response latency for completed requests (includes network + model).
- unit: ms
- aggregation: histogram -> expose p50/p90/p95/p99 in dashboards
- labels: model_id (low-cardinality: e.g., llama-3b, codeparrot), region, tenant_bucket (pre-hashed, < 50 values), route (low-cardinality)
- owner: Priya Nair
- alerting: Sev2 if p95 increases by >30% over rolling-1h baseline or exceeds 1200ms absolute for 5m
- instrumentation: instrument at request controller edge, record both total and model_inference_time spans

2) kvcache.hit_ratio
- description: fraction of cache hits for prefix/KV cache across serving instances
- unit: percent
- aggregation: gauge computed as hits / (hits + misses) at scrape time
- labels: model_family, host_pool
- owner: Mariana Lopes
- alerting: warn when < 60% for sustained 15m on high-throughput models

Label/cardinality rules (practical):
- High-cardinality keys (request_id, full user_id, prompt_hash) MUST never be labels; use logs or attributes in traces instead.
- Tenant identifiers must be bucketed/hashed to <50 buckets for dashboards, and a separate high-cardinality per-tenant export pipeline can be used when customers request it.
- model_version label should be limited to release channels (stable, canary) or short hashes (first 8 chars) at most.
- Use label_allowlist at scrape time for noisy endpoints.

Tracing anchors and conventions (OpenTelemetry friendly):
- Root span: inference.request (attributes: trace.request_id, tenant_bucket, route, model_id, sequence_target)
- Child spans: router.evaluate, batch.coalesce, runtime.kvcache.check (attr: kv_hit=true|false), runtime.kernel.exec, network.send (if applicable)
- Span naming: service.operation (e.g., runtime.kernel.exec)
- Key trace attributes (always): model.id, model.variant, seq_len, token_count, cache_hit (bool), batch_size, tenant_bucket
- Scrubbed tenant info: never put raw tenant/email; always send tenant_bucket or hashed_tenant_id
- Sampling guidance: default 1-2% for global traffic, 100% sampling for traces flagged by errors, and dynamic sampling bump for traces tied to alerting windows (configurable via sampling hook)

Instrumentation notes (code-level best practices):
- Prefer histograms for latency with fixed buckets that reflect our SLOs (e.g., [10,50,100,250,500,1000,2000] ms).
- Emit counters for event totals (requests_started, requests_completed, requests_failed).
- Record both end-to-end and component-level latencies (controller vs model vs network) to avoid blind spots.
- Attach lightweight attributes to metrics (low-cardinality) and push heavy context to spans/logs.
- Example pseudo-code (Python / prometheus client):
  REQUEST_LATENCY = Histogram('inference_request_latency_ms', 'end-to-end latency', buckets=[0.01,0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0,2.0], labelnames=['model_family','region','tenant_bucket'])
  with REQUEST_LATENCY.labels(model_family, region, tenant_bucket).time():
      process_request()

Dashboard hygiene & widget guidance:
- One canonical place per metric: dashboards/metric-catalog link must include canonical queries and short description.
- Widget types: heatmap for latency distribution, timeseries for p90/p95, single stat for current rate and error ratio, table for top contributing routes/models.
- Default time ranges: 1h, 6h, 24h. For expensive widgets (heavy grouped queries) keep 24h to coarse aggregation only.
- Cost tip: avoid exploded-by-tenant default panels; require an extra {show per tenant} click to enable high-cardinality mode.

Alerting & severity mapping (practical):
- Sev1: total outage (>= X% traffic failing or routing blackhole) -> escalate to oncall and paged immediately
- Sev2: severe degradation (SLO risk: p95 latency > threshold or error rate spike causing >10% user-visible failures)
- Sev3: noise/minor regressions (single-model slowdowns with limited traffic) -> ticket and owner slack ping
- Every alert must include: query, window, threshold rationale, playbook link, and runbook steps to collect traces/logs.

Investigation flow (short):
1) Observe symptom (alert or dashboard anomaly).
2) Check cardinal metrics: request.rate, error.rate, p95 latency, backend_cpu/gpu_util.
3) Jump to service-level traces filtered by tenant_bucket and time window +/- 5m. Look for span hotspots (e.g., long runtime.kernel.exec).
4) If trace sampling is low, bump sampling via retrospective trace collector or enable debug sampling for the rolling window.
5) Check recent deploys (git tags, canary rollouts) and model version pins for correlation.
6) If capacity-related, check autoscaler events, instance counts, and queue/backlog metrics.
7) Apply mitigation: rollback, scale up, route traffic to fallback model, or enable reduced-quality quantized model as emergency.
8) File postmortem or notes linked to alert with root cause hypothesis and metric changes (include pre/post graphs).

Onboarding checklist for a new metric (copy this into PR):
- [ ] Add metric to metric-catalog with template filled
- [ ] Add instrumentation with unit tests and export smoke check
- [ ] Create dashboard widget in the canonical team dashboard
- [ ] Add owner and oncall contact in catalog entry
- [ ] Propose alert thresholds and include rationale in PR description
- [ ] Run cost estimate for cardinality retention (metric cardinality x expected series)

Retention & cost guidance:
- Hot metrics (SLO-critical): 30d retain at full resolution, then downsample for 90d+
- Medium importance: 7d full resolution, 30d aggregated
- Churny/debug metrics: short retention (72h) unless explicitly promoted
- Enforce label cardinality caps in collector to avoid runaway series.

Review cadence & ownership responsibilities:
- Owners must review their metrics quarterly for accuracy, cardinality, and alert relevance.
- eng-observability will run a metric-cost report monthly and flag candidates for consolidation.
- Owners are expected to respond within 48h to metric alerts and to open follow-up tickets within 72h when issues are not self-resolving.

Common pitfalls and mitigation patterns:
- Pitfall: adding raw user identifiers as labels -> Mitigation: reject in PR, move to trace attribute and use pre-hashed tenant_bucket label.
- Pitfall: overly aggressive per-request tracing -> Mitigation: use sampling + error-boosted capture and ability to temporarily toggle higher sampling for investigations.
- Pitfall: duplicate metrics with slightly different naming -> Mitigation: prefer canonical metric and deprecate duplicates (add alias mapping in catalog).

Appendix: example trace span map for typical request
- inference.request (root)
  - router.route_evaluate (100-300us)
  - batch.join_wait (0-200ms, depends on batching)
  - kvcache.check (kv_hit=true/false)
  - model.invoke (gpu_time: xx ms)
  - response.serialize (10-50ms)
Key attributes to log on spans: trace.request_id, model.id, model.variant, seq_len, token_count, cache_hit, batch_size, host_pool

Notes / open questions:
- Should we add a standard label for compute_tier (e.g., onprem, prod-gpu-v2, burst) to simplify routing dashboards? (open, @Ethan)
- Proposal: lightweight per-tenant cost metering pipeline outside Prometheus for billing-sensitive customers (design doc needed).

Where to edit this doc:
- This is a living doc. Keep edits in the observability shared drive and update the metric catalog Confluence page when making changes.
- Suggested next steps: build a simple onboarding PR template that enforces metric template fields and cardinality checks at lint time.

Owners & contacts:
- Priya Nair (pri@redwood.ai) — primary contact for latency & model-inference metrics
- Ethan Rhodes (erh@redwood.ai) — batching and request-rate owner
- Mariana Lopes (mlopes@redwood.ai) — KV cache & caching strategy

End of doc.
